newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: News blackout in Philippines on N.Korean defector.
newsitem.headline: News blackout in Philippines on N.Korean defector.

text.p: Mystery surrounded the whereabouts on Wednesday of top North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop after he flew into the Philippines from China amid fears he could be a target of a Pyongyang hit squad.
Checks of various possible hideways for Hwang in this mountain resort north of the Philippine capital Manila yielded no sign of the 73-year-old former senior aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.

Hwang disappeared without a trace after a chartered Air China aircraft flew him on Tuesday into the former U.S. Clark airbase, 80 km (50 miles) north of Manila in a secrecy-shrouded trip from Xiamen, China.
Hwang and at least three companions transferred to two helicopters at Clark and army officials said they had headed for the mountain resort city of Baguio.
Hwang's journey from the South Korean consulate in Beijing, where he had sought asylum on February 12, was shrouded in secrecy as officials spread a smokescreen of confusion.
Officials in Manila said the attempts to block out Hwang's whereabouts were caused by fears of an assassination attempt by North Korean agents.
"The military may be misleading you. Remember that this is a top security operation," one Filipino diplomat, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters on Tuesday.

A Seoul foreign ministry official sought to reasssure South Koreans on Tuesday that Hwang was "secure and safe" in a third country. But even when he reaches Seoul, his security will never be completely assured.
North Korea has a history of deadly attacks against its arch-rival South Korea. The two Koreas are still frozen in Cold War confrontation.

Just three days after Hwang sought asylum in Beijing, a prominent North Korean defector was fatally shot near Seoul. The victim, Li Il-nam, was a nephew of the former wife of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.

Li underwent plastic surgery on his face, changed his name, and restlessly moved from one address to another. But his cover was blown by a local magazine, and on February 15 two suspected Pyongyang agents hunted him down.

Hwang was whisked away from Clark to Baguio, 200 km (125 miles) north of Manila, by two Philippine air force helicopters, according to senior Philipine military officers. But Baguio local officials and police said they had no idea where he was.
"All I know is what I hear from the media," Baguio mayor Mauricio Domogan said. "The military has not told me anything. But they do not have to tell me if it involves security matters."
The Philippine government and the South Korean embassy in Manila clamped a news blackout on Hwang's whereabouts.
"I don't know anything," embassy spokesman Nam Jin-soo said by telephone when asked if the secrecy which veiled Hwang's movements was prompted by fears of a North Korean reprisal.
While there was no official confirmation that Hwang arrived in Baguio, airport sources there said they saw two helicopters arriving at the summer resort city.
Journalists who followed the trail to Baguio said the helicopters were still at the airport there.

Military sources said Hwang could stay in the Philippines from three days to a week. A senior Seoul official said earlier this week that Hwang would stay in a third country "for a considerable period of time" before travelling to South Korea.
Baguio, which was devastated by an earthquake in 1992, is a hill station favoured by Manila's rich and powerful, many of whom own holiday homes there.
Residents said that in recent years it had attracted several religious groups, many of them from South Korea, to set up facilities in the city.
The Philippine presidential summer residence, a military academy and the Camp John Hay resort, a former U.S. military rest recreation centre, are also in Baguio.
Journalists staked out all possible hideaways in Baguio, including the presidential mansion and the Philippine Military Academy.
Both places are in secluded areas that provide ideal shelter for a person such as Hwang, now viewed as a marked man, forever dogged by fear of Pyongyang hitmen.
